title: Conjecture 1 (Berger et al.)
statement_text: There is a function $f$ such that every $t$-local tournament $T$ satisfies $\vec{\chi}(T) \leq f(t)$.
context_text: A tournament is $t$-local if for every vertex $v$ the subtournament induced by the out-neighbors of $v$ has chromatic number at most $t$. The conjecture was raised in Berger et al. [3] as Conjecture 2.6 and settled for $t = 2$ in [7]; the present paper proves it for all $t$.
attributed_to: Berger, Choromanski, Chudnovsky, Fox, Loebl, Scott, Seymour, and Thomassé
paper_contribution: Proves the conjecture for all $t$: every $t$-local tournament has chromatic number at most $f(t) = \max\{(t+1)K,\,(t+1)\ell\}$ for explicit constants $K$ and $\ell$ depending only on $t$, derived via a new result on dominating number and bounded-size subtournaments.

paper_title: Coloring tournaments: from local to global

title: Problem 3
statement_text: For every integer $i \geq 1$, there exists $f(i)$ such that every tournament $T$ with dominating number at least $f(i)$ contains an isomorphic copy of $S_i$.
context_text: The chromatic number $\vec{\chi}(T)$ of a tournament $T$ (its dichromatic number) is the minimum number of colors needed to color the vertices so that each color class induces an acyclic, i.e. transitive, subtournament. A set $S$ of vertices is dominating if every vertex outside $S$ has an in-neighbor in $S$, and the dominating number $\gamma(T)$ is the minimum size of a dominating set. A tournament is $t$-local if the out-neighborhood of every vertex induces a subtournament of chromatic number at most $t$; the paper's main result, answering a conjecture of Berger et al., is that $t$-local tournaments have chromatic number bounded by a function of $t$. A key step is that for every $k$ there are $K$ and $\ell$ such that every tournament with dominating number at least $K$ contains a subtournament on $\ell$ vertices with chromatic number at least $k$. The problem asks whether large dominating number forces a specific high-chromatic subtournament. $S_1$ is the one-vertex tournament and, for $i>1$, $S_i$ is the tournament on $2^i-1$ vertices obtained from a cyclically oriented triangle by blowing up two of its vertices into copies of $S_{i-1}$ (replacing a vertex by a copy of $S_{i-1}$, all arcs to and from it being kept for every vertex of the copy); one can check that $\vec{\chi}(S_i)\ge i$. The problem is trivial for $i\le2$, verified for $i=3$ by Chudnovsky, Kim, Liu, Seymour and Thomassé, and open for all $i\ge4$.

title: Problem 4
statement_text: For every integer $k \geq 1$, there exist integers $K$ and $\ell$ such that every tournament $T$ with dominating number at least $K$ contains a subtournament with $\ell$ vertices and dominating number at least $k$.
context_text: The chromatic number $\vec{\chi}(T)$ of a tournament $T$ (its dichromatic number) is the minimum number of colors needed to color the vertices so that each color class induces an acyclic, i.e. transitive, subtournament. A set $S$ of vertices is dominating if every vertex outside $S$ has an in-neighbor in $S$, and the dominating number $\gamma(T)$ is the minimum size of a dominating set. A tournament is $t$-local if the out-neighborhood of every vertex induces a subtournament of chromatic number at most $t$; the paper's main result, answering a conjecture of Berger et al., is that $t$-local tournaments have chromatic number bounded by a function of $t$. A key step is that for every $k$ there are $K$ and $\ell$ such that every tournament with dominating number at least $K$ contains a subtournament on $\ell$ vertices with chromatic number at least $k$. This problem asks for the analogue of that step with dominating number also in the conclusion. The analogous question with chromatic number in the hypothesis fails for every $k\ge3$: orienting a graph of huge chromatic number and girth larger than $\ell$ along a vertex enumeration (forward along edges, backward along non-edges) gives tournaments of arbitrarily large chromatic number in which every subtournament on $\ell$ vertices has chromatic number at most $2$.

title: Conjecture 7 (Scott and Seymour)
statement_text: For every $k$, there exists $K$ such that if $T$ and $G$ are respectively a tournament and a graph on the same set of vertices with $G$ of chromatic number at least $K$, then there is a vertex $v$ such that $G$ induces on $N^+_T(v)$ a subgraph of $G$ of chromatic number at least $k$.
context_text: Motivated by the paper's main result on out-neighborhoods in tournaments, the authors observe that a suitable notion of 'large' hypergraph would imply a statement about high-chromatic graphs and tournament out-neighborhoods; they note that a very similar conjecture was independently proposed by Alex Scott and Paul Seymour (personal communication [14]).
paper_contribution: Mentioned as a related open conjecture inspired by the paper's main results; the paper provides motivation via the notion of 'large' hypergraphs but offers no proof or partial progress.
notes: Attribution via personal communication [14]; no publication year available.
